item.title: Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks on Local Organisations
item.description:
Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours.

Switzerland ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has now seen these attacks firsthand. In recent days, it received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents. The victims include critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent.” reads the report published by NCSC. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

What stands out is the result. In every AI-assisted attack known to the NCSC, the attackers successfully compromised the victims’ IT systems. The agency sees these incidents as more than isolated cases, warning that they mark a shift in the cyber threat landscape.

The attackers used what the NCSC calls “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”. These AI agents can search for vulnerabilities, choose attack tools, assess the results and decide what to do next, all with limited human input. Security teams also use the same software for penetration testing, which makes these tools dual-use.

The targets aren’t exotic. The agents go after standard or easily guessed passwords, known flaws in software, and systems connected to the internet.

“AI agents often require only a fraction of the time a human would need to locate such vulnerable systems and exploit existing vulnerabilities. Furthermore, they can react flexibly to defence mechanisms by switching to other known attack methods. This leaves organisations with significantly less time to detect an attack and respond appropriately.” continues the report.

AI agents can quickly switch tactics when a defence blocks an attack, leaving organisations less time to detect and stop intrusions. The NCSC warns that these tools speed up common attack methods and that internet-accessible agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI have almost doubled since October 2026. This could lead to more frequent, faster and more successful automated attacks against organisations of all types.

ARTEX isn’t a surprise. The FBI recently published a FLASH alert that describes it as open source, with no model of its own, plugged into external language models. The same advisory says some intrusions went from first contact to privileged access in under three hours.

The NCSC expects more successful attacks and urges companies and critical infrastructure operators to strengthen their security and resilience. It monitors the threat landscape, stays in contact with national and international partners, and shares technical indicators for detecting these tools with infrastructure operators. Its recommendations are short, and it wants them applied without delay.

Start by shrinking what’s exposed. Fewer systems facing the internet means a smaller attack surface, and where possible you can restrict access with geo-blocking or an allow list of IP addresses or network segments. Every internal resource reachable from the internet, such as webmail and VPN, should sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys, with no exceptions.

Then limit the damage. Grant the lowest access rights that work, and watch for deviations from normal behaviour and data volumes across identities, applications, workloads and infrastructure. Test your own infrastructure for vulnerabilities on a regular basis, yourself or with an outside specialist.

“Critical security updates for systems accessible via the internet should be installed as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after release.” concludes the report.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Switzerland)

item.title: U.S. CISA adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
item.description:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the following HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

  • CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability
  • CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability 
  • CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability 

The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score of 7.5), is a path traversal vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration management systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit improper restrictions on file paths to retrieve and read files from the underlying system through the XML interface. Access to sensitive files could provide information useful for further compromising the device. There are no publicly confirmed reports of exploitation in the wild or threat actors associated with this vulnerability. Danfoss addressed the issue in software version 3.3.

The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical improper input validation vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient input validation to execute arbitrary commands on the target system, potentially gaining full control of the affected refrigeration controller. Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability to attacks in the wild or identifying threat actors exploiting it. Danfoss released software version 3.3 to address the issue.

The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score of 8.2), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series systems running software versions prior to 4.2. The authentication bypass allows an attacker to generate web reports without proper authorization, potentially exposing sensitive information such as internal IP addresses, usernames and store names. The vulnerability was identified by researchers at Claroty’s Team82. Although it affects the same family of refrigeration controllers targeted in the European supermarket attacks, there is no public confirmation that attackers exploited this particular CVE during those incidents. Danfoss addressed the vulnerability in software version 4.2.

The fourth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting HPE Juniper Session Smart Conductor. The flaw resides in the AutomatedProvisioner component and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges by supplying a specially crafted Salt minion ID. The vulnerability has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming exploitation in the wild. However, no specific threat actor or ransomware campaign has been publicly attributed to these attacks. Administrators should apply the security updates provided by Juniper, including versions 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 for the affected release branches.

The fifth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability affecting the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. The vulnerability affects MiCollab version 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient file type validation to upload arbitrary files to the target system. Depending on the nature of the uploaded files and the system configuration, this could provide an opportunity for further malicious activity. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified any threat actors associated with this vulnerability. The company released a security patch for affected installations.

The sixth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score of 9.0), is a critical XML injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter validation and leverage malicious content staged in advance to perform XML injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the affected installation. Mitel has not disclosed any confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified threat actors behind attacks exploiting this flaw. A security patch is available for affected MiCollab installations.

The seventh flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score of 5.9), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a specific system-generated random identifier or has access to malicious content staged in advance could exploit the weakness to obtain sensitive information. The vulnerability is limited to the affected functionality and does not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary files elsewhere on the system. No confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been publicly reported. Mitel has released a security patch to address the issue.

The eighth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score of 10.0), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter sanitization to perform blind command injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the affected system. Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity and availability. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or attributed attacks to specific threat actors. A security patch is available to address the vulnerability.

The ninth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. Improper handling of authentication could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass security controls and perform unauthorized actions within the application. Successful exploitation could compromise the security of the affected installation. No publicly confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been reported. Mitel has released a security patch for the affected versions.

The tenth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting Vates Xen Orchestra, a management and backup platform for XCP-ng and XenServer environments. The vulnerability affects versions prior to 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of authentication tokens by supplying a specially crafted cookie containing an empty JSON object. The application may then authenticate the attacker as the owner of an existing, unexpired token. Once authenticated, the attacker could retrieve reusable authentication token identifiers, potentially enabling persistent unauthorized access to the environment. The vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild, although no specific threat actors have been publicly identified. Vates addressed the issue in Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1.

The Danfoss vulnerabilities deserve particular attention because they affect the same family of refrigeration management systems involved in the cyberattacks targeting European supermarkets in October and November 2026.

The first wave of attacks, detected between October 11 and 12, compromised refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail sites in France. Attackers manipulated defrost settings, forcing refrigeration equipment to operate at excessively high temperatures. The incidents resulted in substantial food losses and at least 15 reported fires. A second wave between November 1 and 2 affected retailers across several other European countries.

The French authorities’ investigation attributed the October attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, responsibility for the subsequent November attacks across Europe has not been conclusively established.

The technical evidence points to the exploitation of internet-exposed refrigeration management interfaces, with default credentials and outdated firmware considered likely entry points. However, investigators have not confirmed that CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 or CVE-2025-41450 were specifically exploited during these operations. The incidents instead highlight the risks associated with exposing operational technology (OT) systems directly to the internet without adequate authentication, network segmentation and security updates.

An additional development is worth mentioning: a November 2026 advisory from Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre reported research by Midnight Blue identifying six previously unknown pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, affecting firmware versions up to and including 5.3.2. At the time of the advisory, these flaws had not yet received CVE identifiers and no patches were available. Researchers also warned that attackers could establish persistence surviving factory resets and firmware updates. These findings add another layer of concern to the security of refrigeration infrastructure. ncsc.gov.ie

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA order U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate eight of them by November 28, 2026, and the remaining two by December 9, 2026. The individual deadlines are:

  • November 28, 2026: CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324 and CVE-2026-133469.
  • December 9, 2026: CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2026-133311.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

item.title: 1Password Hacked: Customer Names and Emails Copied, Vaults Untouched
item.description:
1Password says an attacker stole customer names and emails through an employee’s GitHub account, but vaults and passwords remained safe.

1Password has disclosed that an attacker got into some of its backend systems. The company posted its update on November 25 and says customer vaults weren’t affected. It also says some customer account data was copied.

“An attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including the names and email addresses that customers use to sign into 1Password.” reads the update published by 1Password. “Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected. 1Password does not have access to your password or secret keys.”

An attacker accessed some of company’s backend systems and copied a limited amount of customer data. This affected only some customers and included the names and email addresses they use to sign in. The identity security firm has not said how many customers were affected, a detail also missing from TechCrunch’s report.

The attack started with an employee’s corporate GitHub account. 1Password began investigating on November 19, after detecting signs that someone had accessed the account without permission. The attacker used it to access source code and add malicious code to backend services. These services then downloaded customer-related administrative data. It is still unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s GitHub account.

The copied records include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, and the times each account was created and last signed in. They also hold public keys, which are public by design, and Secure Remote Password parameters, which can’t be used to access an account. The rest is non-secret metadata about 1Password’s internal architecture, such as numeric version and file identifiers.

One item deserves more attention: tokens from emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery. A token only completes the process when it’s paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address.

“The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits.” continues the report. “This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.”

Even so, 1Password changed the code format. It now uses ten letters and numbers instead of six digits. This makes it almost impossible for attackers to guess the code by trying different combinations.

Provisioning invitations are used for the SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning services. A small number of users were in the provisioning process during the incident, and 1Password has contacted them directly. The company also says it found no evidence that anyone used the exposed tokens to take over accounts.

The attacker also accessed more than customer records. They copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, which stores secrets used to run 1Password’s infrastructure. The company says its source code does not contain customer data or user secrets. It has also changed all credentials that may have been exposed.

The company says services, availability and product security weren’t affected. Vaults and the items in them weren’t touched, and neither were the keys that protect them or the account recovery keys. 1Password’s apps and browser extensions weren’t affected either, and it doesn’t store account passwords or Secret Keys.

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.” states the report.

To mitigate the incident. 1Password disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token and removed the access the attacker created. It restored clean versions of the affected service, rotated or revoked the internal credentials, tightened its GitHub, CI/CD and endpoint controls, and added detections for this kind of attack. It also brought in independent experts to check its containment and remediation.

Several questions remain open; the company hasn’t disclosed how many customers were impacted or whether they’ve all been notified. At this time it is unclear who is behind the athe attacker is, or whether anyone has made demands. The Hacker News also describes the attacker only as unknown.

For customers, 1Password says there’s nothing to update in your account. It does ask you to watch for unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations or account recovery attempts you didn’t start. Phishers read the news too.

Legitimate messages follow a simple rule: only enter your password or Secret Key in the official 1Password app or website. Always open the app yourself or type the website address manually. You only need your Secret Key the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. If someone asks for it at any other time, treat it as suspicious. You can report suspicious messages to [email protected].

1Password says it will update its post if it discovers anything new. The company has also published its Security Whitepaper since 2015, giving users more information about how it protects their data.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

They also hold public keys, which are public by design, and Secure Remote Password parameters, which can’t be used to access an account. The rest is non-secret metadata about 1Password’s internal architecture, such as numeric version and file identifiers.

One item deserves more attention: tokens from emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery. A token only completes the process when it’s paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address.

“The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits.” continues the report. “This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.”

Even so, 1Password changed the code format. It now uses ten letters and numbers instead of six digits. This makes it almost impossible for attackers to guess the code by trying different combinations.

Provisioning invitations are used for the SCIM Bridge and Hosted Provisioning services. item.title: Australia’s Flight Centre Data Breach Exposes Customer Records and Passport Details
item.description:
Australia’s Flight Centre is investigating a third-party breach that exposed customer travel records and limited passport details.

Australia’s Flight Centre Travel Group is investigating a cyber incident involving a third-party accommodation booking system that may have exposed a significant number of customer records. The company disclosed the incident on November 26, saying it had detected unusual activity in a platform used by several of its leisure travel brands.

The breach affects the accommodation system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout and some independent agents. Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings, which rely on separate systems, haven’t been affected.

According to Reuters, the company has not yet determined how many records were taken. Its initial investigation found that most of the accessed records contained customer names, while some also included basic travel details.

“Flight ⁠Centre said some of its leisure travel brands — the Flight ​Centre brand, Travel Associates and Cruiseabout — and some independent agents ​used the third-party accommodation booking system. The company said the unusual activity did not affect flight bookings.” Reuters states. “The company said it had not yet ​determined how many records the activity extracted, but its initial ​review showed most accessed records contained only customer names, while some also ‌included ⁠basic travel information”

The exposed data may include more sensitive information. Flight Centre believes a very small number of records contained passport details, email addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth. In rare cases, records may also have included health or mobility information, which can be particularly sensitive when linked to travel plans.

So far, the company has found no evidence that credit card, payment or bank account details were accessed. However, the exposed personal and travel information could still be used for targeted scams, identity theft and social engineering attacks.

The incident highlights a common problem with third-party suppliers. A booking platform may store customer information collected by several brands and independent travel agents. This means that a single attack on a shared system could expose data belonging to several businesses at once.

Flight Centre has activated its incident response plan and is investigating the incident with the supplier and cybersecurity firm Mandiant. The company says it is working to identify affected systems, contain the incident, improve security, change authentication keys and passwords, and increase monitoring. It is also notifying the relevant authorities and working with external security experts.

The investigation is still ongoing, and the company has not confirmed how many customers were affected or when the suspicious activity started. Flight Centre says existing hotel bookings can go ahead as planned and that it will contact customers whose data may have been exposed.

For customers, the main concern is how attackers could use the stolen information. An email mentioning a real hotel, booking reference or travel date can look genuine, especially when it arrives shortly before a trip.

Flight Centre has advised customers to be careful with unexpected emails, phone calls or messages about their bookings. They should avoid clicking links, opening attachments or sharing personal information, passwords or payment details in response to unsolicited requests.

The warning is worth taking seriously even if no payment data was exposed. Travel details provide context that criminals can use to make phishing attempts more credible, and a request to “confirm” a booking or passport detail may be the next step in an attack.

Flight Centre said it would contact affected customers and apologised for the concern the incident may cause.

“Flight Centre is warning customers to be cautious of “unexpected emails, calls or messages” about their bookings, and to “not click on links, open attachments or share personal information, passwords or payment details in response”. ABC News states.

“The company apologised to affected customers, noting “that an incident like this can be unsettling”.”

item.title: Linux/EasyShell: MalwareMustDie Identifies One of the Earliest Publicly Documented RATs Built for LoongArch Linux
item.description:
MalwareMustDie analyzes Linux/EasyShell, a Rust implant targeting Linux and macOS, with LoongArch support and stealth features to evade detection.

This case began with a shell script found on a victim’s node, which the author credits to 0xrb. MalwareMustDie’s researcher first read it as one more Chinese miner-style uninstaller or downloader. It wasn’t. The script installs software, and what it delivers is a Rust beacon implant.

MalwareMustDie wrote four reverse engineering notes, one forensics note, and two OSINT notes, then merged them into one report.

That restraint shapes everything that follows. This careful approach guides the entire analysis. The stager is hosted at hxxps://192[.]3.31[.]148:8443 and installs a payload called polkitd on both Linux and macOS. On Linux, it is saved as /usr/bin/polkitd, while on macOS it is placed in ~/Library/Caches/polkitd. The stager randomly chooses one of eight possible file names. The same server hosts the malware and receives its beacon communications over TCP port 8443. It is hosted by ColoCrossing (AS36352) in the United States.

The server provides seven different builds: l32, l64, l128, a32, a64, darwin_amd64 and darwin_arm64. The researcher describes the Linux x86 version, l32, as a Rust-based HTTPS beacon with all its required libraries built into the executable. Its build paths contain references to the EasyShell framework, including strings such as easyshell-http-beacon-implant and impl-core. For this reason, the researcher identifies the malware as Linux/EasyShell.

The l128 build targets LoongArch, a CPU architecture, and was compiled with rustc 1.96.0, while the others use 1.95.0. According to the researchers, this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations he could find in public reporting, identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family.

“I would like to note that this is one of the earliest publicly documented LoongArch64 RAT implementations I could find in public reporting (as of 2026-11-21), identified within the EasyShell multi-platform Rust implant family. “Earliest” here only means that I found no earlier public analysis; the LoongArch build itself is a framework default (chapter 7 addendum).” states the report. “Hands-on access: shell, file theft, credential plugins, SOCKS and relay pivot High. No monetisation code. Operator intent unknown (18.1). The macOS and LoongArch builds are framework defaults offered by every EasyShell stager, not a choice of this operator (18.2).”

Two caveats weaken any story about a targeted LoongArch campaign. The report says the macOS and LoongArch payloads aren’t this operator’s choice, because every EasyShell server offers them by default. The author also doubts the LoongArch build would load on a stock Debian loong64 or Kylin host without matching links or a compatible loader, and says it may never have been tested on real hardware.

The author didn’t run any sample. The beacon is an HTTPS POST to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header and a Windows Chrome 131 user agent. According to the report, the implant can open a remote shell, run plugins and scripts, upload and download files, and zip folders. It also offers SOCKS5 and relay tunnels, an outbound proxy, screenshots, process listing and killing, and self-deletion.

Credential dumping, token elevation and browser password theft aren’t built in. They come from a separate “Extensions” plugin set. The implant also checks for sandboxes, looking at DMI data, hypervisor names, mouse activity and system resources. Then it renames itself like a kernel thread, for example [kworker/0:0].

A third-party Joe Sandbox run on November 21 gives a useful reality check. It executed another l32 copy on Ubuntu 20.04 for about five minutes. The copy had the same size, 3,769,372 bytes, but a different hash, and it made three TCP connections to the C2, forked a child that called prctl, uname and a thread sleep, and created an empty hidden file. The score was 2 out of 100 with no YARA or Suricata match, which says more about the malware waiting for someone else to show up than about its harmlessness.

That hash difference matters. The server writes random bytes into one slot of every payload it generates, so each victim gets a different file.

“YARA family rule MMD_Linux_EasyShell_Rust_Implant on memory dumps and new binaries (it still matches the builds without the crate name); do not rely on the hashes for other victims.” MalwareMustDie warns.

The first draft of the report dates from November 19, and an addendum on November 22 documented the per-download hashes and the developer repository.

On attribution, the author is careful. EasyShell is a Chinese red team C2 framework sold through trial and member programs, and its public repository matches the samples. It isn’t VShell and has no Kinsing or SystemTen link, although the stager is based on a VShell template. No operator is named, and the author says the tool’s build markers describe its build environment, not whoever runs this C2.

There’s one loose thread. A separate chapter describes an intrusion on a Chinese mobile-malware hosting server, and a single shell-history line there re-ran the EasyShell stager from the same C2. The author rates the link between the two operators as medium confidence. A note about a December 2025 incident that used the same stager template at a different IP is marked unverified.

For security teams, the l32 version does not have its own way to remain on an infected system, although its plugins may add this feature. The researcher suggests looking for processes that use names normally associated with kernel threads, such as [kworker/0:0] or [rcu_sched], but have a real executable file listed under /proc/pid/exe. Another warning sign is HTTPS POST traffic to /api/v2/sync with an X-Client-Id header.

On macOS, defenders should look for executable files in user Caches folders that lack a quarantine attribute, code signatures without a Team ID, and security permission requests (TCC prompts) that mention polkitd.

The report also includes YARA, Sigma and osquery detection rules. The researcher recommends starting in detection-only mode. These rules were tested against known malware strings, but not against a large collection of legitimate software to check for false positives.

If a system looks infected, there is one important rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread immediately. The researcher recommends first isolating and preserving the system before terminating any process.

The report ships YARA, Sigma and osquery rules, meant to start in detect-only mode. They were checked on strings, not through a full retro-hunt on legitimate software.

“Golden rule: do not kill the fake kernel thread first. Collect its process state and memory, freeze it, cut its network, then clean. Killing it first loses the live config, the session keys and the tunnel table.” concludes the report.

item.title: Drupal Warns of New Critical Flaw Exploited in the Wild
item.description:
Drupal fixes a critical flaw exploited in the wild that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites.

Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites.

Tracked as CVE-2026-136716, the flaw is related to improper handling of unusual or incomplete installation states. It is connected to CVE-2026-132165, also known as Fail2Install, which Drupal patched on November 18. However, the previous fix did not address every vulnerable installation scenario.

“SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.” Drupal maintainers warned.

The issue affects websites where the Drupal installer (install.php) remains remotely accessible. Drupal stressed that the vulnerability does not affect sites where administrators have already properly secured the installer.

One particularly concerning aspect is that administrators cannot easily identify affected installations through the Drupal interface. Moreover, sites that have already been compromised may no longer appear to be in the vulnerable state.

Drupal confirmed that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and urged administrators to investigate possible compromises.

“This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.” continues the advisory.

Recommended actions include reviewing logs for unauthorized access and unexpected changes involving the main administrative account, known as user 1. Administrators should also verify that its email address is under their control and consider resetting its password.

The vulnerability has been addressed in the following releases:

  • Drupal 11.4.x: Update to 11.4.14
  • Drupal 11.3.x: Update to 11.3.23
  • Drupal 10.6.x: Update to 10.6.23

Drupal 11.0.x through 11.2.x and 10.5.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive security fixes.

After updating, administrators should run update.php to fix affected installation states and ensure that the installer is properly secured on all existing and new websites.

Drupal’s own usage statistics provide further evidence of the exposure. Data published on November 15, 2026, show that thousands of websites still report running Drupal 8.x and tens of thousands use Drupal 9.x, both unsupported branches. Although these figures cover only sites reporting their versions through Drupal’s update system, they highlight the persistence of outdated installations and the need for organizations to migrate to supported releases.

This week, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Drupal Core flaw CVE-2026-132165 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

item.title: FIFA Confirms a Cyberattack, Hackers Claim 12 GB of Internal Files
item.description:
FIFA confirms a cyberattack exposing personal and business data, while the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claims responsibility for the breach.

FIFA confirmed it was the victim of a cyberattack, threat actors gained access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information.” The organization told The Associated Press it’s working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.

FIFA did not disclose technical details about the attack or what kind of information hackers accessed.

A hacking group, which calls itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club, claimed the security incident before FIFA made its announcement. The threat actors shared a screenshot on X showing what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, the group appeared to claim responsibility for the attack in a reply to a post reporting that more than 12 GB of FIFA internal documents had been leaked.

At this moment, the group’s X account has been suspended, and their Tor leak site is unreachable.

“FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” states the organization. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”

The breach comes at a sensitive time for FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, who faces criticism over a failed plan to sell World Cup stakes to private investors and his bid to extend his presidency to 2031.

He remains the favorite ahead of the March 18 election, against Kohzo Tashima and Philippe Diallo. The AP report does not link the cyberattack to these issues. FIFA warns that the exposure of personal data could have serious consequences for those affected.

“Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.” concludes the AP.

Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) is a newly emerged ransomware and data-extortion group first observed in November 2026. Threat intelligence platforms recorded its first activity on November 19, when it listed three organizations on its data-leak site: US-based firearms manufacturer Smith & Wesson, healthcare provider UCHealth, and telecommunications company Frontier Communications. On November 20, the group added FIFA to its victim list, bringing the number of publicly recorded claims to four.

item.title: SAP Security Incident: Stolen Tokens Raise Supply Chain Concerns
item.description:
SAP confirms a security incident as reports point to stolen GitHub tokens and altered source code. Data breach remains unconfirmed.

SAP has confirmed a security incident, and most of the details come from the press, not from the company. The global enterprise found suspicious activity in its IT systems. DER SPIEGEL reported that attackers stole company employees’ access tokens and used them to change and copy source code on GitHub.

“According to information obtained by SPIEGEL, the software manufacturer SAP is now dealing with an incident. The perpetrators may have used AI systems for assistance.” reads the report published by DER SPIEGEL.

The German software maker says it took immediate steps to protect customers and secure its services.

SAP says investigators had found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data at that stage. It didn’t answer detailed questions about the incident. An internal memo cited by Spiegel calls the incident active, and SAP is reportedly handling the investigation under the name “Project Granite”.

Sources inside the software giant also told Spiegel that the attackers may have used AI agents. SAP has not confirmed this, and it is still unclear whether AI played any role in the attack. For now, this should be treated as an unconfirmed report.

Employees were reportedly told not to discuss the incident. The report also says SAP management does not believe it needs to inform customers proactively. SAP reportedly told German broadcaster Tagesschau that customer data was not affected.

SAP has not disclosed how the attackers obtained the employees’ tokens. Cybersecurity News recently reported a separate case in which a malicious VS Code extension stole GitHub tokens, but there is no evidence linking that attack to the SAP incident.

SAP publishes source code for its products and open-source projects on GitHub. However, the report does not say which repositories were affected or whether the stolen code was public or private. This information is important to understand the impact of the incident.

GitHub’s audit log guidance explains how organizations can trace recorded actions back to a compromised token, and administrators can revoke credentials by user and token type.

item.title: Air Force Cloud One Breach: Updates Blocked, Migration Paused, Scope Unknown
item.description:
Reuters reports a breach of the US Air Force’s Cloud One. The scope, attackers and data stolen remain unknown; updates are blocked.

Reuters reports that hackers have breached Cloud One, one of the US Air Force ‘s main cloud computing platforms. The breach could put a large amount of sensitive military data at risk, including information about military operations, personnel, and logistics.

Two sources said the intrusion was discovered about a month ago during work to upgrade the platform. The discovery has disrupted the entire service. Reuters could not identify the attackers, determine how much of the platform was affected, or confirm whether any data had been stolen.

“Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told ​Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.” Reuters states.

“does not comment on the ​security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems.” reads a statement sent to Reuters by the Air Force. “We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems ​and mission capabilities.”

Cloud One started in 2017 as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs. It combines the resources of four operators, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet, to run scores of applications, including ones for personnel data, pay, logistics and maintenance. Two of the sources say it’s among the military’s biggest cloud platforms.

Two applications show why the breach is serious. Cloud-Based Command and Control brings together air defense radar data and other information from across North America. The Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 US Air Force locations worldwide.

SAIC was the main contractor until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to Reuters, while Leidos referred questions to the Air Force. According to one source, investigators have asked US Cyber Command, the military’s cyber unit, to assess the damage. Cyber Command did not respond to Reuters either.

“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources told Reuters.

The disruption is already visible. Two sources, plus a fourth person familiar with the matter, say efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused. A fifth source says some users had their administrator rights revoked.

The timing makes the incident more serious. Updates to applications running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to install fixes. This happened just as several serious software vulnerabilities were being disclosed across the technology industry. All five sources spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.

According to one source, the attackers exploited a software flaw to access the platform’s control plane, which manages its main functions. The source compared it to a universal remote control.

“Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry.” Reuters continues. “A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.”

The breach lands amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions. Cloud networks are a particular worry because AI models can swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas. The US government is already dealing with at least six other recently disclosed incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.

item.title: Fake Government App Exposes Italy’s Expanding Spyware Surveillance Industry
item.description:
A fake Interior Ministry app used Morpheus spyware to target asylum seekers in Italy, raising questions about surveillance and oversight.

An Android app called FirmaDigitale promised asylum seekers news on their protection status, instead, it was delivering spyware.

An IrpiMedia investigation by Rosita Rijtano builds on Lookout’s 2024 discovery and attributes the malware to IPS, a Latina supplier to prosecutors, police and intelligence agencies. Nobody knows who ordered the operation or whom it hit.

Victims downloaded the app from firmadigitale.assistenza-mobile[.]it, a page mimicking the website of Italy’s primary postal service provider Poste Italiane. The app displayed the Interior Ministry logo and mentioned a protection decree. Police deny any link to it, and Poste didn’t comment.

The spyware could add components to use the microphone, intercept internet calls, record the screen and track the phone. It could also reach contacts, call logs, files and texts. The site has been unreachable since 2025, but the app could still circulate elsewhere.

Osservatorio Nessuno named the spyware Morpheus in April 2026 after finding it in a fake Fastweb app. Attackers also abused the TIM, Iliad, PosteMobile and WindTre brands, and Iliad said it knew of no such apps. Morpheus can even hijack WhatsApp through a fake biometric prompt.

“We are faced with yet another example of low-cost spyware that exploits vulnerability and suffering to strike at one of every individual’s most intimate rights: the privacy of the devices we use daily for all our activities and communications,” comments a spokesperson for Osservatorio Nessuno, a volunteer organization that studies digital surveillance technologies and provides technical assistance to journalists and activists.

“This case is particularly cruel because it leverages—from a position of supreme power—systems that are already discriminatory and hostile, specifically targeting migrants. The responsibility lies in many quarters: from the complete lack of Italian or European regulation regarding the proliferation of such companies, to a total absence of transparency and constraints—including ethical ones—on these types of operations.”

Kristina Balaam of Citizen Lab, formerly at Lookout, says social engineering makes these tools cheaper than zero-click spyware and still effective. Why burn a rare exploit when a convincing form will do?

Osservatorio Nessuno blames weak Italian and European rules, opacity and missing ethical limits. Civil liberties coalition Cild wants to know why authorities would target asylum seekers, who authorized it and what it produced.

IPS has plenty of company, including RCS, Area, SIO and Innova. Nine established firms reported €214.4 million in 2024 revenue from surveillance and intelligence tools. Italy supplied 72.8% of revenue among the five disclosing geography.

Spyware targets rose from 2,894 in 2021 to 5,611 in 2025, up about 94%. Mafia cases accounted for 2,930 last year, ordinary crimes for 2,618 and terrorism for 63. Germany authorized 91 spyware operations in 2024 and carried out 57.

Italian law permits spyware well beyond mafia and terrorism cases, including corruption and many ordinary crimes. Defence lawyer Eugenio Losco warns that a criminal association charge opens the door, even against unionists and activists. Interception spending also reached about €299 million in 2025, despite a national price list meant to cut costs.

Controls remain thin. Italy has no prior quality check, and authorities lack the skills to verify the software. In the eSurv case, a company kept intercepts on its own servers, and its trial continues.

Magistrates’ association vice president Marcello De Chiara calls spyware essential and current safeguards for its use adequate. He wants tighter rules for private vendors, including a national register and clearer ownership.

The concern extends beyond this app. A researcher says at least five activists recently received spyware links, while Sea-Watch’s Giorgia Linardi has reported zero-click surveillance in 2021. IrpiMedia doesn’t tie either case to FirmaDigitale.

Lawyer Giovanni Battista Gallus says Italy lacks a complete law limiting what spyware can do. Collected data can remain archived, and authorities needn’t notify targets when an investigation is shelved. IrpiMedia captures the result, that targets may never find out, in one sentence:

“Those who are spied upon may never even find out. In fact, there is no obligation to notify an individual that they have been subjected to surveillance once an investigation is closed.” Gallus concludes. “Furthermore, while the surveillance tools must be deactivated at the end of an operation, the material collected is not automatically deleted; instead, it may remain stored in the public prosecutor’s archives.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Morpheus spyware)
